content: Blood type A, also referred to as a blood group, is a classification of blood based on the presence or absence of inherited antigenic substances on the surface of red blood cells (RBCs). These antigens can be proteins, carbohydrates, glycoproteins, or glycolipids, depending on the blood group system. Some of these antigens are also found on the surface of other cell types in various tissues. Certain red blood cell surface antigens, which originate from a single allele or closely linked genes, collectively form a blood group system. The immunological effects of mismatched blood transfusions are more likely to involve components of the ABO blood group system or the RhD antigen (also known as the Rhesus factor or Rhesus D antigen) of the Rhesus blood group system than components of other blood group systems. Therefore, in routine blood bank preparation for transfusion, the presence or absence of the immunogenic blood group antigens—A antigen, B antigen, and RhD antigen—is always determined for both donor and recipient blood. A capital letter (A, B, or O) refers to the ABO blood group, while positive or negative refers to the presence or absence of the RhD antigen. In routine donor blood preparation and selection for transfusion, it is not necessary to determine the status of other blood group antigens or antibodies. This is because antibody screening and cross-matching (or computer-aided simulated cross-matching) prior to transfusion detect any other blood group incompatibilities between donor blood and intended recipients. If an individual is exposed to a blood group antigen that is not recognized as self, their immune system will produce antibodies that specifically bind to that antigen, forming immunological memory against it. This process sensitizes the individual to that blood group antigen. These antibodies can bind to antigens on the surface of transfused red blood cells (or other tissue cells), often leading to cell destruction through the recruitment of other immune system components. When IgM antibodies bind to transfused cells, the cells may clump together (agglutinate). It is critical to select compatible blood for transfusions and compatible tissue for organ transplantation. Transfusion reactions involving minor antigens or weak antibodies may cause minor issues, but more serious incompatibilities can trigger a robust immune response, resulting in massive RBC destruction, low blood pressure, and even death. Blood types are inherited and represent contributions from both parents. Pregnant women often carry a fetus with a different blood type, and in some cases, the mother may form antibodies against the fetal red blood cells, causing hemolysis of fetal RBCs. This can lead to low fetal blood counts, a condition known as hemolytic disease of the newborn (HDN). Some blood types are associated with the inheritance of other diseases. For example, the Kell antigen is linked to McLeod syndrome. Certain blood types may also influence susceptibility to infections, such as the resistance to specific malaria species observed in individuals lacking the Duffy antigen. The Duffy antigen, likely due to natural selection, is less common in ethnic groups from regions with a high incidence of malaria. The two most significant blood group systems were discovered during early experiments with blood transfusion: the ABO group in 1901 and the Rhesus group in 1937. The development of the Coombs test in 1945, the advent of transfusion medicine, and the understanding of hemolytic disease of the newborn led to the discovery of additional blood groups. Today, the International Society of Blood Transfusion (ISBT) recognizes 29 human blood group systems. A complete blood type describes the full set of 29 substances on the surface of RBCs, and an individual's blood type is one of many possible combinations of blood group antigens. Across the 29 blood groups, over 600 different blood group antigens have been identified, though many are rare or primarily found in specific ethnic groups. An individual's blood type typically remains the same throughout life, but in rare cases, it can change due to the addition or suppression of an antigen during infection, malignancy, or autoimmune disease. Blood types have been used in forensic science and paternity testing, but these applications are being replaced by DNA analysis, which provides greater accuracy. The ABO blood group system is the most important blood group system in human blood transfusion. The associated anti-A and anti-B antibodies are usually of the Immunoglobulin M (IgM) type. These antibodies are produced in the first years of life through sensitization to environmental substances such as food, bacteria, and viruses. The O in ABO is often referred to as 0 (zero/null) in other languages. The Rhesus blood group system is the second most significant blood group system in human blood transfusion. The most important Rhesus antigen is the RhD antigen, as it is the most immunogenic of the five main Rhesus antigens. RhD-negative individuals typically do not have anti-RhD IgG or IgM antibodies because these antibodies are not usually produced through sensitization to environmental substances. However, RhD-negative individuals can produce IgG anti-RhD antibodies following a sensitizing event, such as a fetomaternal transfusion of blood from a fetus during pregnancy or, occasionally, a blood transfusion with RhD-positive RBCs. The ISBT currently recognizes 29 blood group systems, including the ABO and Rhesus systems. In addition to ABO and Rhesus antigens, many other antigens are expressed on the RBC surface membrane. For example, an individual can be AB RhD positive and simultaneously M and N positive (MNS system), K positive (Kell system), Lea or Leb negative (Lewis system), and so on, being positive or negative for each blood group system antigen. Many blood group systems were named after the patients in whom the corresponding antibodies were first identified. Transfusion medicine is a specialized branch of hematology that focuses on the study of blood groups and the work of blood banks to provide transfusion services for blood and other blood products. Blood products must be prescribed by a licensed medical doctor, similar to medications. In the USA, blood products are tightly regulated by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Blood banks routinely test blood from both donors and recipients to ensure compatibility and safety. If incompatible blood is transfused, severe acute immunological reactions, hemolysis (RBC destruction), renal failure, and shock are likely to occur, with death being a possibility. Patients should ideally receive their own blood or type-specific blood products to minimize the risk of a transfusion reaction. Risks can be further reduced by cross-matching blood, although this step may be skipped in emergencies. Cross-matching involves mixing a sample of the recipient's blood with a sample of the donor's blood and checking for agglutination (clumping). If agglutination occurs, that donor's blood cannot be transfused to that recipient. Blood banks must ensure that all blood specimens are correctly identified, and labeling has been standardized using a barcode system known as ISBT 128. Rare blood types can cause supply challenges for blood banks and hospitals. For example, Duffy-negative blood is more common in people of African origin, and its rarity in other populations can lead to shortages for patients of African ethnicity. Similarly, RhD-negative individuals may face risks when traveling to regions where RhD-negative blood is scarce, such as East Asia. A pregnant woman can produce IgG blood group antibodies if her fetus has a blood group antigen that she does not possess. This can occur due to a small fetomaternal hemorrhage during childbirth or obstetric intervention, or sometimes after a therapeutic blood transfusion. This can lead to Rh disease or other forms of hemolytic disease of the newborn (HDN) in the current or subsequent pregnancies. If a pregnant woman is known to have anti-RhD antibodies, the RhD blood type of the fetus can be tested by analyzing fetal DNA in maternal plasma to assess the risk of Rh disease. Some blood group antibodies can cause severe HDN, while others may only cause mild HDN or are not known to cause HDN. Blood banks fractionate whole blood into several products to maximize the benefit of each donation and extend shelf life. Common products include packed RBCs, plasma, platelets, cryoprecipitate, and fresh frozen plasma (FFP). FFP is quick-frozen to retain labile clotting factors V and VIII, which are administered to patients with potentially fatal clotting problems caused by conditions such as advanced liver disease, anticoagulant overdose, or disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC). Packed red cells are made by removing as much plasma as possible from whole blood units. Modern recombinant methods are now used to synthesize clotting factors for hemophilia, avoiding the risks of infection transmission associated with pooled blood products. Blood group AB individuals have both A and B antigens on their RBCs and no antibodies against A or B antigens in their serum. Therefore, they can receive blood from any group (preferably AB) but can donate only to other AB individuals. Blood group A individuals have the A antigen on their RBCs and IgM antibodies against the B antigen in their serum. They can receive blood only from groups A or O (preferably A) and can donate to groups A or AB. Blood group B individuals have the B antigen on their RBCs and IgM antibodies against the A antigen in their serum. They can receive blood only from groups B or O (preferably B) and can donate to groups B or AB. Blood group O individuals lack A and B antigens on their RBCs but have IgM anti-A and anti-B antibodies in their serum. They can receive blood only from group O individuals but can donate to individuals of any ABO blood group (A, B, O, or AB). In emergencies, O-negative blood can be issued if processing the recipient's blood would cause a detrimental delay. Plasma compatibility is the reverse of RBC compatibility. Plasma from type AB blood can be transfused to individuals of any blood group, while type O plasma can only be used by type O recipients. RhD antibodies are uncommon, so donor plasma issued by blood banks is typically free of RhD antibodies and other atypical antibodies, making it suitable for RhD-positive or RhD-negative recipients as long as ABO compatibility is maintained. Individuals with type O-negative blood are often called universal donors for whole blood or packed RBC transfusions, while those with type AB-positive blood are called universal recipients. However, these terms are oversimplifications, as they do not account for reactions to other blood group antigens or antibodies. For example, transfusing O RhD-negative blood into an A RhD-positive recipient may not cause a reaction between the recipient's anti-B antibodies and the transfused RBCs. However, the small amount of plasma in the transfused blood may contain anti-A antibodies, which could react with the recipient's A antigens, though significant reactions are unlikely due to dilution factors. In April 2007, a method was discovered to convert blood types A, B, and AB to O using enzymes. This method is still experimental and has not undergone human trials. It specifically removes or converts antigens on RBCs but does not address plasma compatibility. Blood types have also been used in popular culture, such as the Japanese blood type theory of personality, which links ABO blood types to personality traits. This belief, while popular in Japan and parts of East Asia, is dismissed by scientists.
